reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Cholesteatoma is a collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear cleft; despite the name it contains neither cholesterol nor a tumour
It is characteristically associated with attic or posterosuperior marginal perforations, which is why this is called the unsafe or atticoantral type of chronic otitis media
Typical symptoms are scanty, foul-smelling ear discharge with progressive conductive hearing loss
Otoscopy may reveal a retraction pocket, whitish debris or granulations and a crust in the attic; a polyp or aural granulation should raise suspicion
It is locally destructive because the matrix and surrounding inflammation erode bone, threatening the ossicles, facial nerve, labyrinth and dura
Congenital cholesteatoma can occur behind an intact drum with no history of infection
Imaging with high-resolution CT maps disease extent and bony erosion, and MRI (including diffusion-weighted sequences) helps detect or confirm residual or recurrent disease
The mainstay of treatment is surgical eradication by mastoidectomy and tympanoplasty, since medical therapy alone cannot cure it
reference.pathophysiology: Cholesteatoma consists of a sac of keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (matrix) that sheds keratin into the middle ear and mastoid, where it accumulates and cannot escape. Acquired disease most often follows persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction that produces a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida or posterosuperior pars tensa; trapped desquamated epithelium enlarges the pocket, or squamous epithelium migrates through a marginal perforation. The expanding mass and its associated chronic inflammation release enzymes and mediators that resorb surrounding bone, progressively destroying the ossicular chain and eroding toward the facial nerve, semicircular canals and intracranial cavity. Superimposed infection produces the characteristic foul discharge and accelerates the destructive process.
additionalDifferentials: Keratosis obturans of the external canal
Aural polyp or granulation from other causes
Middle ear or external canal malignancy
Glomus tumour of the middle ear
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and microscopy to identify retraction pockets, keratin debris and granulations
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to define extent and bony erosion
Diffusion-weighted MRI to detect residual or recurrent cholesteatoma
Pure tone audiometry to document conductive or mixed hearing loss
Culture of discharge to guide treatment of secondary infection
Fistula test if erosion into the labyrinth is suspected
redFlags: Vertigo or a positive fistula sign suggesting labyrinthine erosion
Facial nerve weakness indicating involvement of the facial canal
Severe headache, fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting intracranial complication (an emergency)
Sudden worsening of hearing or new sensorineural loss
Postauricular swelling or abscess signalling spread beyond the mastoid
reference.prognosis: With complete surgical removal the disease can be controlled and complications prevented, but cholesteatoma has a tendency to recur or leave residual matrix, so long-term follow-up is essential; neglected disease leads to serious intratemporal and intracranial complications.
pitfalls: Dismissing scanty foul discharge as trivial and missing an unsafe ear
Failing to inspect the attic and posterosuperior quadrant where retraction pockets hide
Relying on medical treatment alone when surgery is needed for cure
Not recognising an aural polyp as a possible marker of underlying cholesteatoma
Neglecting long-term surveillance for residual or recurrent disease
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Definitive treatment is surgical eradication of disease by mastoidectomy, either canal-wall-up or canal-wall-down, with complete removal of the keratin matrix
Reconstruct the ossicular chain and repair the tympanic membrane with ossiculoplasty and tympanoplasty to restore hearing
Control secondary infection pre-operatively with aural microsuction toilet and topical antibiotic-steroid ear drops
Undertake surveillance for residual or recurrent disease with second-look surgery or diffusion-weighted MRI
Manage or pre-empt complications such as facial nerve involvement, labyrinthine fistula and intracranial extension urgently
Provide hearing rehabilitation with hearing aids where surgical reconstruction is insufficient
Maintain long-term ENT follow-up given the tendency to recur or leave residual matrix
